lessons.title: వసంత ఋతువు, వేసవి, వానాకాలం, శీతాకాలం — the pattern completes itself
lessons.gloss: spring, summer, monsoon, winter — completing the Dravidian pattern of native heat/rain words plus Sanskrit spring

segments.text: Telugu closes out the Dravidian season words the same way Kannada did: native words for summer/rain/cold, and a spring-word borrowed twice over from Sanskrit.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The words

utterances: Telugu: వసంత ఋతువు (vasanta ṛtuvu). meaning: "spring". source: both vasanta and ఋతువు ṛtuvu ("season") are Sanskrit, like Kannada's pair.
Telugu: వేసవి (vēsavi). meaning: "summer". source: native Dravidian — cousin of Kannada's bēsige.
Telugu: వానాకాలం (vānākālam). meaning: "rainy season". source: వాన vāna ("rain," native) + kālam ("time," itself Sanskrit-derived but long assimilated).
Telugu: శీతాకాలం (śītākālam). meaning: "winter/cold season". source: śīta ("cold") leans Sanskrit-flavored here, unlike Tamil/Kannada's fully native cold-words.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: Be honest about the pattern, one more time

segments.text: Telugu's vēsavi and Kannada's bēsige are close enough in shape to be genuine cousins — the same native Dravidian summer-word wearing two languages' sound changes. And once again, it's వానాకాలం (vānākālam, the rains) that actually organizes Andhra/Telangana's agricultural year, not a clean four-way Western split — the same honest point its neighbours make.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "vēsavi" — summer, cousin of Kannada's bēsige]

segments.instruction: "vānākālam" — the rains, the real central season

segments.text: What's the relationship between Telugu's vēsavi and Kannada's bēsige? (Cousins — the same native Dravidian summer-word.) Which Dravidian languages borrow BOTH halves of their spring-word from Sanskrit (the season-name AND the word for "season" itself)? (Kannada and Telugu — vasanta ṛtu(vu) — unlike Tamil/Malayalam's single vasantham loan plus the long-assimilated kaalam.)
